title: Global Citizenship
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about what it means to be a citizen of the world -- how globalisation reshapes identity and belonging, and how to act globally while acting locally.
competenceGoals: discuss how globalisation affects citizenship, identity, and belonging
reflect on how young people can participate and influence society at local, national, and global levels

content.content:
## A citizen of where?

Climate change does not respect passports. Pandemics spread across continents in weeks. Information travels the globe in seconds. In an increasingly connected world, the very question of what it means to be a citizen has begun to stretch beyond national borders. Many people now think of themselves not only as citizens of a particular country, but as citizens of the world.

This chapter explores that expanding idea. We will look at what **global citizenship** means and how it relates to national citizenship, how globalisation has changed our understanding of identity and belonging, the role of international frameworks like the UN Sustainable Development Goals, and the genuine debates about the benefits and limitations of thinking globally. The central insight is that being connected to a wider world brings not only new opportunities but also new responsibilities -- and that you do not need to travel far to take them on.

## Global citizenship and the roots of an old idea

**Global citizenship** is the idea that all people belong to a single global community and have responsibilities toward one another that go beyond national borders. A global citizen is someone aware of the wider world, who respects and values diversity, understands how the world works economically and politically, takes responsibility for their actions, and is willing to act to make the world more equitable and sustainable. Importantly, global citizenship does not *replace* national citizenship -- rather, it adds another layer of identity and responsibility. What does it look like in everyday life? It might be a student in London buying Fairtrade coffee, following international news and reducing plastic use; an engineer in Canada working with Doctors Without Borders and pushing for sustainable supply chains; or a teenager in Australia joining climate strikes, learning about Indigenous perspectives and fundraising for UNICEF. Global citizenship is not about being wealthy or well-travelled -- it is about recognising that your actions have consequences beyond your immediate community and being willing to act accordingly.

This is not a new idea. It has deep philosophical roots in **cosmopolitanism**, a tradition stretching back to ancient Greek thought, where the Stoics believed that all people are citizens of the cosmos. In modern usage, cosmopolitanism is the idea that all human beings belong to a single moral community, regardless of nationality, ethnicity or religion, and that we have moral obligations to people beyond our own borders -- to strangers as well as neighbours. This perspective underpins much of the thinking behind global citizenship, international human rights and humanitarian aid. It is worth presenting in a balanced way: cosmopolitanism is an appealing ideal, but it sits in genuine tension with the strong, particular attachments people feel to their own nations and communities -- a tension that runs through many debates about globalisation, identity and belonging.

content.content:
## Identity, belonging and acting locally

Globalisation has fundamentally changed how we think about identity and belonging. In the past, most people's identity was closely tied to their local community and nation; today, many people feel multiple, overlapping identities. Cultural exchange means music, food, fashion and ideas cross borders more easily than ever -- a Norwegian teenager might listen to American hip-hop, eat Japanese sushi and watch Korean television. Migration means over 280 million people live outside their country of birth, many holding dual citizenship or feeling connected to multiple countries. Digital connectivity creates communities based on shared interests rather than shared geography, and education through exchange programmes and online learning exposes young people to different cultures. But a balanced account also recognises the tensions: some people embrace multiple identities, while others feel globalisation threatens national culture and values; debates about immigration often centre on questions of identity and belonging; and the rise of nationalism in many countries can be seen as a reaction against globalisation. Even the spread of English as a global lingua franca, spoken by an estimated 1.5 billion people, raises genuine questions -- is it a form of connection, or of cultural dominance? Presenting both possibilities fairly is part of thinking clearly about a complex change.

The phrase "think globally, act locally" captures an important truth: you do not need to travel the world to be a global citizen, because many of the most meaningful actions happen in your own community. Global issues have local connections -- reducing your carbon footprint contributes to a global climate effort, volunteering at a local food bank addresses global supply-chain injustices, welcoming newcomers in your school is a form of global solidarity, and learning about other cultures prepares you to be a global citizen. International frameworks support this connection: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights establishes rights for all people, the UN Sustainable Development Goals provide a shared agenda, the Paris Agreement unites nations against climate change, and UNESCO works to build peace through education, science and culture. English-speaking countries -- the USA, UK, Canada, Australia and others -- play significant roles in global governance through the UN, NATO and the Commonwealth, and their policies on trade, immigration, climate and aid have global consequences. That is precisely why active, informed citizenship in these countries is a matter of global importance, and why the small choices made locally can ripple far beyond home.

questions.solution: Globalisation has led many people to feel multiple, overlapping identities, shaped by cultural exchange, migration, digital connectivity and education.

options.text: That you must travel the world to make a difference
That meaningful global action can happen in your own community
That local issues do not matter

questions.solution: "Think globally, act locally" means you do not need to travel the world to be a global citizen, because many meaningful actions happen in your own community.

options.text: Because English is the only language
Because it can be seen as both connection and cultural dominance

questions.task: Which international framework provides a shared agenda for tackling global challenges?
questions.solution: The UN Sustainable Development Goals provide a shared global agenda for tackling challenges, alongside frameworks like the UDHR and the Paris Agreement.

content.content:
## In short

In a connected world where climate change and pandemics cross every border, the idea of citizenship has stretched beyond nations toward global citizenship -- the recognition that all people belong to a single global community with shared responsibilities, adding to rather than replacing national identity. This rests on the old philosophy of cosmopolitanism, an appealing ideal that nonetheless sits in tension with strong national and community attachments. Globalisation has transformed identity and belonging, giving many people overlapping identities while provoking reactions like rising nationalism. The principle "think globally, act locally" shows that meaningful global action starts at home, supported by frameworks like the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Because English-speaking countries shape global governance, informed citizenship within them carries consequences far beyond their own borders.
